holidays.name: Something on a Stick Day
holidays.description: A day devoted to eating anything and everything that can be skewered, from corn dogs and kebabs to chocolate-dipped bananas and fair-food oddities. If it can be impaled on a stick, it deserves a spot at the party.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food observance that grew out of state fair and carnival culture, where putting food on a stick makes it portable and easy to eat while walking around. It is commonly listed on March 28 in food-holiday calendars.
holidays.funFact: The corn dog is often credited to the 1940s, with several vendors claiming to have invented it, and today fairs compete each year to create the wildest food on a stick, including fried butter and deep-fried pickles.

holidays.name: Respect Your Cat Day
holidays.description: A day for humans to show proper deference to their feline overlords by offering treats, respecting their personal space, and accepting that the cat is in charge of the household.
holidays.origin: An informal pet-themed observance that appears on March 28 in many quirky holiday calendars, celebrating the independent and sometimes snobby nature of cats.
holidays.funFact: Cats spend roughly 70 percent of their lives sleeping, which means they may spend most of Respect Your Cat Day napping through the tribute.

holidays.name: Weed Appreciation Day
holidays.description: A day to rethink the humble weed, honoring dandelions, clover, and other plants that gardeners love to hate. Participants are encouraged to appreciate the toughness, beauty, and sometimes edible qualities of these uninvited garden guests.
holidays.origin: An unofficial nature and gardening observance that encourages people to see weeds as resilient wildflowers rather than enemies, noting that the label is mostly about where a plant happens to be growing.
holidays.funFact: Dandelions are edible from root to flower, with the leaves used in salads, the flowers in wine and fritters, and the roots roasted as a coffee substitute.

holidays.name: Barnum and Bailey Day
holidays.description: A celebration of the circus spirit, honoring the showmen behind the Greatest Show on Earth with clowns, acrobats, and a bit of larger-than-life spectacle.
holidays.origin: Tied to the partnership between P.T. Barnum and James A. Bailey, whose circuses merged in 1881 to create the famous Barnum and Bailey Circus, a staple of American entertainment for generations.
holidays.funFact: Barnum's circus once featured Jumbo the elephant, whose name became a common word for anything enormous, which is why we now have jumbo shrimp and jumbo jets.

holidays.name: Neighbor Day
holidays.description: A day for stepping across the fence and actually saying hello to the people next door by sharing a baked good, a wave, or a cup of borrowed sugar.
holidays.origin: A friendly community observance, often listed on March 28 in the United States, meant to build stronger neighborhoods and encourage people to know the folks living near them.
holidays.funFact: Studies on community life often find that people who know their neighbors report feeling safer and more connected, proving that borrowing a ladder can be good for your health.
